topics.name: Electronegativity
topics.kicker: How hard an atom pulls on shared electrons · Makes bonds polar
topics.briefing: Electronegativity measures how hard an atom tugs on the electrons it shares in a chemical bond, like one team in a tug-of-war. Linus Pauling built the first scale for it in 1932, and fluorine tops his chart at nearly 4. When two atoms pull unequally, the shared electrons drift toward the stronger puller, which is why the oxygen end of a water molecule is slightly negative.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Robert Mulliken defined this quantity as the average of an atom’s first ionization energy and its electron affinity. A different scale for this quantity, created by Allred and Rochow, is based on the pull of the effective nuclear charge felt at an atom’s covalent radius.
tossups.r: Fluorine has the highest value of this quantity. For 10 points, name this measure of how strongly an atom attracts the electrons it shares in a bond.

tossups.p: In 1932, a chemist built the first scale for this property by comparing bond dissociation energies, measuring how much stronger a bond between two different atoms is than expected. Values on that scale have no units, and the highest is nearly 4.
tossups.r: Linus Pauling created that scale. This property increases from left to right across the periodic table. For 10 points, name this tendency of an atom to pull bonding electrons toward itself.

tossups.p: Trifluoroacetic acid is a far stronger acid than acetic acid because of an inductive effect caused by fluorine’s high value of this property. Differences in this property put partial positive and partial negative charges on the two ends of a polar bond.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, measured on a scale by Linus Pauling, that describes how strongly an atom pulls on the electrons it shares.

tossups.p: Beryllium and aluminum behave alike partly because they have nearly equal values of this property, an example of the diagonal relationship on the periodic table. Cesium and francium have the lowest values of this property, while noble gases like neon are often left off its scales.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which is highest for fluorine, that measures an atom’s pull on shared electrons.

tossups.p: Leland Allen proposed a scale for this property based on the average energy of an atom’s valence electrons. Two atoms of the same element, as in a chlorine molecule, have equal values of this property, so they share their electrons equally in a nonpolar bond.
tossups.r: Fluorine’s value of this property on Pauling’s scale is nearly 4. For 10 points, name this measure of how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.

tossups.p: Cesium fluoride has the largest difference in this property of any compound made of two nonradioactive elements, so its bonding is strongly ionic. When chemists assign oxidation numbers, all of the shared electrons in a bond are counted for the atom with the higher value of this property.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, symbolized by the Greek letter chi [“KYE”], that measures an atom’s attraction for the electrons in a bond.

tossups.p: Hydrogen bonds form when hydrogen is attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, small atoms with high values of this property. Because oxygen ranks second only to fluorine in this property, the oxygen end of a water molecule carries a partial negative charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which describes how strongly an atom attracts the electrons it shares in a bond.

tossups.p: Many chemistry textbooks say that when two atoms differ in this property by more than about 1.7 on Pauling’s scale, the bond between them is ionic. Carbon and hydrogen are close enough in this property that their bonds are considered nearly nonpolar.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that increases across a period and decreases down a group, measuring an atom’s pull on bonding electrons.

tossups.p: This property is a central idea of _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_, a book by the scientist who won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his research on chemical bonding. Elements with low values of this property, such as sodium and potassium, are often called electropositive.
tossups.r: That scientist, Linus Pauling, made its best-known scale. For 10 points, name this property, highest for fluorine, that measures how strongly an atom draws shared electrons toward itself.

tossups.p: Chlorine releases more energy than fluorine when it gains an electron, yet fluorine beats chlorine in this related property, which deals with electrons shared inside a bond. Robert Mulliken calculated this property by averaging ionization energy and electron affinity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that Linus Pauling put on a scale on which fluorine has the highest value.

tossups.p: The most common modern value of this property for fluorine is 3.98, and the values have no units because they only compare atoms with one another. Oxygen comes second in this property, followed by chlorine and nitrogen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which tells how strongly an atom attracts shared electrons and explains why some covalent bonds are polar.

tossups.p: The Allred–Rochow scale for this property depends on the effective nuclear charge felt by an atom’s outer electrons. This property generally decreases going down a group, because the outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus and are shielded by inner electrons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, highest near the upper right of the periodic table at fluorine, that measures an atom’s pull on bonding electrons.

tossups.p: Because only differences in this property can be found from bond energies, the chemist who built its best-known scale chose hydrogen as a reference point, and hydrogen’s value on that scale is now listed as 2.20. A very large difference in this property between two atoms, as in sodium chloride, means one atom essentially pulls the electrons away from the other.
tossups.r: The result is an ionic bond. For 10 points, name this property that measures how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons.

tossups.p: Oxygen has a positive oxidation number only in compounds with fluorine, such as oxygen difluoride, because fluorine is the only element with a higher value of this property. Fluorine’s value of this property is so high that it has an oxidation number of negative 1 in all of its compounds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property that increases from left to right across a period, which measures how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons.

tossups.p: Carbon dioxide’s bonds are polar because oxygen beats carbon in this property, but the molecule has no overall dipole moment, since its two oxygen atoms pull equally in opposite directions. This property is often written with the Greek letter chi [“KYE”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which is highest for fluorine and lowest near cesium, measuring an atom’s pull on bonding electrons.

clues.t: Measures how strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a chemical bond toward itself
Fluorine has the highest value of any element, nearly 4 on the most common scale
Linus Pauling created the first and most widely used scale for it in 1932
Increases from left to right across a period and decreases going down a group
The difference between two atoms’ values tells whether a bond is ionic, polar covalent, or nonpolar covalent
Unequal pulling gives the two ends of a polar bond partial charges (δ+ and δ−), making a dipole
Cesium and francium, in the lower left corner of the periodic table, have the lowest values
Oxygen is second only to fluorine, followed by chlorine and nitrogen
Hydrogen bonds form when hydrogen is attached to nitrogen, oxygen, or fluorine, small atoms that pull hard on electrons
Noble gases like helium and neon are often left off the scale because they rarely form bonds
Elements with low values, such as sodium, potassium, and the other alkali metals, are called electropositive
Often written with the Greek letter chi (χ); values on Pauling’s scale have no units
In assigning oxidation numbers, shared electrons are counted for the atom with the higher value
Many textbooks treat a difference of more than about 1.7 on Pauling’s scale as an ionic bond
Carbon (2.55) and hydrogen (2.20) are so close that C–H bonds are nearly nonpolar
Pauling based his scale on bond dissociation energies: the extra strength of an A–B bond compared with A–A and B–B bonds
Pauling used hydrogen as his reference point; its value on his scale is now listed as 2.20
Robert Mulliken’s scale averages an atom’s first ionization energy and its electron affinity
The Allred–Rochow scale uses the pull of the effective nuclear charge at an atom’s covalent radius
Leland Allen’s scale uses the average energy of an atom’s valence electrons
Two atoms of the same element, as in a chlorine molecule, have equal values, so they share electrons equally in a nonpolar bond
Inductive effect: fluorine atoms pull so hard that trifluoroacetic acid is far stronger than acetic acid
Diagonal relationship: beryllium and aluminum have nearly equal values, so they behave alike
Cesium fluoride has the largest difference of any compound made of two nonradioactive elements, so its bonding is strongly ionic
Pauling explained it in _The Nature of the Chemical Bond_ and won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Fluorine is always −1 in compounds, and oxygen is positive only when bonded to fluorine, as in oxygen difluoride
Chlorine has a higher electron affinity than fluorine, but fluorine still pulls harder on shared electrons
Carbon dioxide has polar bonds but no overall dipole, because its two oxygen atoms pull equally in opposite directions

trap.title: Not electron affinity!
trap.body: Electron affinity is the energy change when a single, lone gas atom gains an extra electron; this property is about an atom’s pull on electrons it shares inside a bond. The two follow similar trends across the periodic table, so they are easy to mix up, but they are different answers. In fact, chlorine, not fluorine, has the highest electron affinity of any element. Ionization energy, the energy needed to pull an electron off, is another close cousin.
trap.fix: Listen for “shared electrons,” “bonds,” “Pauling,” “polar,” or the Greek letter chi: that means this property. “Energy released when an atom gains an electron” means electron affinity, and “energy needed to remove an electron” means ionization energy.
trap.line: Real answer line: Electronegativity (do not accept “electron affinity”)

topics.name: Iron
topics.kicker: Element 26 · The metal in steel, blood, and Earth’s core
topics.briefing: Iron is the metal that built the modern world: mix in a little carbon and it becomes steel, the stuff of skyscrapers, bridges, and cars. It is the most common element in the whole Earth by mass, packed into the planet’s core, and its reddish oxide, better known as rust, gives Mars its color. Inside your blood, iron in hemoglobin carries oxygen to every cell.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Ferrocene, a famous “sandwich compound,” has one atom of this element sitting between two flat rings of five carbon atoms. The deep-blue pigment Prussian blue, first made in Berlin in the early 1700s, is a compound of this element.
tossups.r: Its two common ions are called ferrous and ferric. For 10 points, name this metal with atomic number 26, the main ingredient in steel.

tossups.p: In the thermite reaction, powdered aluminum reacts with an oxide of this element, giving off so much heat that this element comes out molten and can be used to weld railroad tracks together. The Haber process for making ammonia uses a catalyst based on this element.
tossups.r: This element rusts in moist air. For 10 points, name this metal, the main component of steel.

tossups.p: This element’s isotope with mass number 56 has one of the highest binding energies per nucleon of any nucleus. A massive star builds up a core of this element that cannot release energy by fusing, so the core collapses and the star explodes in a supernova.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 26, the most common element in Earth by mass.

tossups.p: At room temperature, this metal has a body-centered cubic crystal form called ferrite, but at high temperatures it changes into a face-centered cubic form called austenite [“AW-stuh-nite”]. Austenite can dissolve far more carbon than ferrite can.
tossups.r: Adding a small amount of carbon to this metal makes steel. For 10 points, name this element, whose chemical symbol comes from the Latin word ferrum.

tossups.p: The mineral goethite [“GUR-tite”], named after the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, is made of this element, oxygen, and hydrogen. Pyrite, a shiny brass-colored mineral nicknamed “fool’s gold,” is a compound of this element and sulfur.
tossups.r: Its main ores include hematite and magnetite. For 10 points, name this metal, the main ingredient of steel.

tossups.p: Some bacteria release molecules called siderophores [“SID-ur-uh-forz”] to capture this element from their surroundings. In the human body, the protein ferritin stores this element, and the protein transferrin carries it through the blood.
tossups.r: This element sits at the center of each heme group in hemoglobin. For 10 points, name this metal that helps red blood cells carry oxygen.

tossups.p: This element loses its strong magnetism when heated above its Curie temperature, about 770 degrees Celsius. Early compasses used pieces of lodestone, a naturally magnetized form of the mineral magnetite, which contains this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this magnetic metal with atomic number 26, whose Latin name gives us the word “ferromagnetism.”

tossups.p: Henry Bessemer developed a process that blew air through this molten metal to burn away extra carbon, making steel cheap enough for railroads and skyscrapers. Before that step, this metal’s ore was heated with coke and limestone in a blast furnace.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal, which rusts when it is exposed to oxygen and water.

tossups.p: The Eiffel Tower, completed in 1889, was built from thousands of pieces of a wrought form of this metal. A rich ore of this metal, hematite, gets its name from the Greek word for blood because of its reddish color.
tossups.r: An oxide of this metal gives Mars its red color. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 26.

tossups.p: This transition metal sits in group 8 of the periodic table, between manganese and cobalt. Stainless steel is made by adding chromium, and often nickel, to this metal so that it resists rusting.
tossups.r: A diet that is too low in this element can cause anemia. For 10 points, name this metal found in hemoglobin.

tossups.p: Adding thiocyanate [“thy-oh-SY-uh-nate”] ions to a solution containing this element’s plus-3 ions produces a blood-red color, a classic laboratory test. This element’s plus-2 and plus-3 ions are called ferrous and ferric, and both kinds appear together in the mineral magnetite.
tossups.r: This metal rusts when it combines with oxygen and water. For 10 points, name this main ingredient of steel.

tossups.p: This element ranks only fourth by mass in Earth’s crust, behind oxygen, silicon, and aluminum. Earth’s magnetic field is generated by the churning liquid outer core, which is made mostly of this element mixed with nickel.
tossups.r: Measured by mass, this element is the most common in Earth as a whole. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 26, the main ingredient in steel.

tossups.p: The planet Mercury has an unusually large core made mostly of this metal, and dust containing an oxide of this metal gives Mars its reddish color. Some meteorites are made mostly of this metal mixed with nickel.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this metal, the main element in Earth’s core and in steel.

tossups.p: Cytochromes [“SY-toh-krohmz”] in the electron transport chain contain heme groups built around this element, which switches between two charge states as it passes electrons along. Myoglobin, the protein that stores oxygen in muscles, also contains this element.
tossups.r: Each heme group in hemoglobin holds one atom of it. For 10 points, name this metal that helps blood carry oxygen.

tossups.p: A dagger found in the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh Tutankhamun has a blade made from this metal that came from a meteorite. In the Middle East and Europe, the Bronze Age was followed by an age named for this metal, when tools and weapons made from it became common.
tossups.r: Steel is made by mixing this metal with a small amount of carbon. For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 26, which rusts in moist air.

clues.t: Element with atomic number 26; its symbol comes from the Latin word ferrum
Main ingredient of steel, an alloy made by adding a small amount of carbon
Rusts when it reacts with oxygen and water, forming a reddish-brown oxide
Sits at the center of each heme group in hemoglobin, the blood protein that carries oxygen
Makes up most of Earth’s core, mixed with nickel, and is the most common element in Earth by mass
Strongly magnetic; the word ferromagnetism comes from its Latin name
Its main ores are hematite and magnetite; lodestone is naturally magnetized magnetite
Smelted from ore in a blast furnace with coke and limestone, which removes impurities as slag
The Bessemer process (1850s) blew air through the molten metal to burn off carbon and make cheap steel
An oxide of it in the dust gives Mars its red color; Mercury has an unusually large core of it
Massive stars build a core of it that cannot be fused for energy, so the core collapses in a supernova
Its +2 and +3 ions are called ferrous and ferric; the mineral magnetite contains both
A transition metal in group 8, period 4, between manganese and cobalt
Stainless steel adds chromium, and often nickel, to keep it from rusting
Too little of it in the diet can cause anemia, a shortage of healthy red blood cells
Ferrocene, a “sandwich compound,” has one atom of it between two flat five-carbon rings
The deep-blue pigment Prussian blue, first made in Berlin in the early 1700s, is one of its compounds
Thermite reaction: aluminum plus its oxide makes molten metal, used to weld railroad tracks
The Haber process for making ammonia uses a catalyst based on it
Its isotope with mass number 56 has one of the highest binding energies per nucleon of any nucleus
Its room-temperature body-centered cubic form is called ferrite; its high-temperature face-centered cubic form is austenite
It loses its strong magnetism above its Curie temperature, about 770 °C
The mineral goethite, named after the writer Goethe, contains it; pyrite (“fool’s gold”) is its compound with sulfur
Bacteria release siderophores to grab it; the protein ferritin stores it, and transferrin carries it in the blood
Its +3 ion turns blood-red when thiocyanate is added, a classic lab test
Cytochromes in the electron transport chain, and myoglobin in muscles, contain heme groups built around it
The Eiffel Tower (1889) is built from thousands of pieces of its wrought form
A dagger in Tutankhamun’s tomb has a blade made of it from a meteorite; some meteorites are mostly this metal and nickel

trap.title: Element, not steel
trap.body: Steel is an alloy made mostly of this element plus a little carbon, so clues about the Bessemer process, skyscrapers, or stainless steel tempt players to say “steel.” But steel is a mixture, not an element. Cobalt and nickel are the other traps: they come right after this element on the periodic table, they are also magnetic, and nickel joins it in Earth’s core and in many meteorites.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element” or “this metal,” never say steel. Atomic number 26, hemoglobin, rust, “ferrous” and “ferric,” and the Latin word ferrum all point here; cobalt is element 27 and nickel is element 28.

topics.name: Avogadro’s number
topics.kicker: About 6.02 × 10²³ · The number of particles in one mole
topics.briefing: Avogadro’s number is about 602 sextillion (6.02 × 10²³), the number of atoms or molecules in one mole, the chemist’s supersized version of a “dozen.” Just 18 grams of water, a little more than a tablespoon, holds that many molecules. Chemistry fans celebrate Mole Day every October 23 from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m., and since 2019 the number has been fixed at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³.
topics.answerHtml: Avogadro’s number (accept Avogadro’s constant or NA; prompt on Avogadro alone or on the value 6.02 × 1023)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Jean Perrin gave this number its name in 1909 and measured it by tracking the jittery Brownian motion of tiny particles, work that earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. Albert Einstein had shown in 1905 how Brownian motion could be used to find it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in one mole, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Dividing the Faraday constant, about 96,485 coulombs per mole, by the charge of a single electron gives this constant. Robert Millikan’s oil-drop measurement of that electron charge let scientists calculate this constant much more accurately.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, roughly 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd, which counts the particles in a mole.

tossups.p: Johann Josef Loschmidt [“LOHSH-mit”] made one of the first estimates of this quantity in 1865, working from the size of gas molecules. Before 2019, this quantity equaled the number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in one mole, about 6.022 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Scientists pinned down this constant by counting the atoms in nearly perfect, polished spheres of silicon-28, using X-rays to measure the spacing of the atoms in the crystal. In 2019, the mole was redefined so that it depends on an exact value of this constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd per mole.

tossups.p: At the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress, Stanislao Cannizzaro revived an 1811 hypothesis by this number’s namesake, helping chemists agree on atomic weights. That namesake, an Italian count, said that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd, of particles in a mole.

tossups.p: One gram equals about this many daltons, or atomic mass units, which is why a substance’s molar mass in grams per mole matches the mass of one of its molecules in daltons. About 18 grams of water contain this many molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in one mole, roughly 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: At standard temperature and pressure, about 22.4 liters of any ideal gas contain this many molecules, whether the gas is helium, oxygen, or carbon dioxide. That fact follows from a hypothesis made in 1811 by this number’s namesake.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd, of particles in a mole.

tossups.p: When this quantity is treated as a constant rather than a pure number, it has units of “per mole.” Multiplying the number of moles in a sample by this quantity gives the number of atoms or molecules in the sample.
tossups.r: Mole Day is celebrated on October 23 in its honor. For 10 points, name this number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein’s 1905 doctoral thesis estimated this number by studying how dissolved sugar molecules make water thicker, or more viscous. Multiplying this number by the charge of one electron gives the Faraday constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in one mole, roughly 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Dividing a substance’s molar mass by this constant gives the mass of a single atom or molecule of that substance. Because its value was fixed exactly in 2019, this constant no longer has any measurement uncertainty.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this constant, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd per mole.

tossups.p: Depositing one mole of silver metal by electrolysis takes this many electrons, which together carry about 96,485 coulombs of charge. Just as a dozen means 12 of something, a mole means this many of something.
tossups.r: Chemists honor it every October 23 on Mole Day. For 10 points, name this number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Tiny grains of a yellow resin called gamboge [“gam-BOHJ”], settling in water while gravity battled the jostling of Brownian motion, let Jean Perrin measure this number. Those experiments helped convince scientists that atoms are real.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in a mole, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: This number explains why about 12 grams of carbon, 18 grams of water, and 2 grams of hydrogen gas all contain the same number of particles: each sample is one mole.
tossups.r: October 23 is celebrated as Mole Day in its honor. For 10 points, name this number, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: This constant is named for a scientist born in Turin in 1776, the same year as the Declaration of Independence, who never measured the constant himself. That scientist’s hypothesis about gases was largely ignored until after his death.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number of particles in one mole, about 6.02 times 10 to the 23rd.

tossups.p: Dividing the ideal gas constant, about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, by the Boltzmann constant gives this constant, which links gas laws written for single molecules to gas laws written for whole moles.
tossups.r: Since 2019, its value has been exactly 6.02214076 times 10 to the 23rd. For 10 points, name this constant, the number of particles in a mole.

clues.t: Its value is about 6.02 × 10²³ (6.02 times 10 to the 23rd)
Tells how many particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) are in one mole of a substance
Named for an Italian count who studied gases in the early 1800s
Mole Day is celebrated every October 23, from 6:02 a.m. to 6:02 p.m.
Before 2019, it equaled the number of atoms in exactly 12 grams of carbon-12
Since the 2019 redefinition of SI units, it is fixed at exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ per mole
Treated as a constant rather than a pure number, it has units of “per mole”
About 22.4 liters of an ideal gas at standard temperature and pressure (0 °C, 1 atm) hold this many molecules
About 18 grams of water, which is one mole, contain this many molecules
One gram equals about this many daltons (atomic mass units), so molar mass in grams matches molecular mass in daltons
Dividing a substance’s molar mass by it gives the mass of a single atom or molecule
Its namesake’s 1811 hypothesis: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules
Its namesake was born in Turin in 1776 and never measured it himself
Jean Perrin named it in 1909 and measured it using Brownian motion, winning the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics
Perrin watched tiny grains of gamboge resin settle in water, balancing gravity against Brownian motion
Albert Einstein showed how to calculate it in 1905, in his doctoral thesis on sugar solutions and his paper on Brownian motion
Johann Josef Loschmidt made one of the first estimates of it in 1865, from the size of gas molecules
The Faraday constant (about 96,485 coulombs per mole) equals it times the charge of one electron
Robert Millikan’s oil-drop measurement of the electron’s charge let scientists calculate it accurately
Depositing one mole of silver by electrolysis takes this many electrons
The ideal gas constant R (about 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin) equals it times the Boltzmann constant
Scientists counted the atoms in nearly perfect spheres of silicon-28, using X-rays to measure the spacing between atoms
Stanislao Cannizzaro revived its namesake’s hypothesis at the 1860 Karlsruhe Congress

trap.title: Number, law, or mole?
trap.body: This number’s namesake also names a separate answer line, Avogadro’s law: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. The mole is the other trap: the mole is the unit (like “a dozen”), while this is the count of particles in one mole. Saying just “Avogadro” only earns a prompt.
trap.fix: A value (6.02 × 10²³), Mole Day, Perrin, the Faraday constant, or silicon spheres means the number, also called the constant. “Equal volumes of gases” means Avogadro’s law, and “this unit” means the mole. Always finish with “number” or “constant.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Avogadro’s number (accept Avogadro’s constant or NA; prompt on Avogadro alone or on the value 6.02 × 1023)

topics.name: Halogens
topics.kicker: Group 17 of the periodic table · The “salt-forming” elements
topics.briefing: The halogens are the six elements of group 17: fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine, and tennessine. Their name means “salt-former,” because they react eagerly with metals to make salts, like the sodium chloride on your dinner table. Fluorine is the most reactive element of all, chlorine keeps swimming pools clean, and bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
topics.answerHtml: Halogens (accept group 17 or group VIIA elements; prompt on group 7)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henri Moissan [“mwah-SAHN”] won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for isolating the lightest of these elements, which he finally managed in 1886 by electrolysis. The heaviest of these elements, tennessine, was first made in 2010 and named for a U.S. state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, including fluorine and chlorine, whose atoms have seven valence electrons.

tossups.p: The second-lightest of these elements has the highest electron affinity of any element, even higher than the lightest one. The lightest of these elements forms a surprisingly weak bond with itself, weaker than the bond between two atoms of the second-lightest.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of reactive elements, whose name means “salt-former,” that includes fluorine and chlorine.

tossups.p: With hydrogen, the members of this group form acids, and only the one made with the lightest member, which can etch glass, is a weak acid. Two different members of this group can bond together in compounds like chlorine trifluoride.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements that gain one electron to form ions with a −1 charge, such as chloride and bromide.

tossups.p: Astatine, the rarest naturally occurring member of this group, was first made at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1940, and its name comes from the Greek word for “unstable.” Its lighter neighbor in this group, iodine, is named for the Greek word for “violet.”
tossups.r: These diatomic elements sit just left of the noble gases. For 10 points, name this group that includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

tossups.p: Bernard Courtois [“koor-TWAH”] discovered one of these elements in the ashes of seaweed in 1811. Antoine Balard [“bah-LAR”] announced the discovery of another one in 1826, and its name comes from the Greek word for “stench.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, including iodine and bromine, which form salts when they react with metals.

tossups.p: Silver compounds of these elements are so sensitive to light that they made old-fashioned photographic film work, and a silver compound of one of them is sprayed into clouds to help make rain or snow.
tossups.r: Iodine is added to table salt to keep the thyroid gland healthy. For 10 points, name this group of elements whose name means “salt-former.”

tossups.p: Thomas Midgley Jr. helped develop refrigerants called CFCs, which contain two of these elements and were later phased out by the 1987 Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer. These elements become less reactive going down their group.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, including fluorine and chlorine, that form salts with metals.

tossups.p: Some very bright light bulbs contain a small amount of iodine or bromine, which helps their glowing tungsten filaments last longer. Chlorine, another member of this group, is used to disinfect swimming pools and drinking water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements whose atoms have seven valence electrons and form ions with a −1 charge.

tossups.p: The heaviest member of this group, element 117, was first made in 2010 by a team of Russian and American scientists and named for the state of Tennessee. Another member of this group, astatine, is radioactive and extremely rare.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements that also includes fluorine, chlorine, bromine, and iodine.

tossups.p: Two different members of this group can bond to each other, forming compounds such as chlorine trifluoride and iodine heptafluoride. Moving down this group, the atoms get larger and the elements become less reactive.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, each of which needs just one more electron to fill its outer shell.

tossups.p: When chlorine water is added to a solution of potassium bromide, the mixture turns orange-brown because chlorine pushes out the less reactive member of this group, an example of a displacement reaction.
tossups.r: Fluorine is the most reactive member of this group. For 10 points, name this group of elements whose name means “salt-former.”

tossups.p: At room temperature, the lightest two members of this group are gases, the third is a reddish-brown liquid, and the fourth is a gray-black solid that turns directly into a violet vapor when heated.
tossups.r: These elements react with sodium to form salts such as table salt. For 10 points, name this group of elements just left of the noble gases.

tossups.p: Grignard [“green-YAR”] reagents are made by reacting magnesium metal with a carbon compound containing one of these elements, such as bromine. Fluorine, the most reactive member of this group, is also the most electronegative element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of elements, including chlorine and iodine, whose atoms have seven valence electrons.

tossups.p: Humphry Davy proved that one of these elements was an element, not a compound, and named it after the Greek word for “pale green.” Carl Wilhelm Scheele [“SHAY-luh”] had first produced that element in 1774.
tossups.r: These elements form salts with metals like sodium. For 10 points, name this group of elements that includes chlorine, fluorine, and iodine.

tossups.p: Roy Plunkett accidentally discovered the nonstick plastic Teflon in 1938, and it is made of carbon and the lightest of these elements. Iodine, another member of this group, is added to table salt to keep the thyroid gland healthy.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this group of reactive elements with seven valence electrons each.

clues.t: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine, astatine, and tennessine
The column just left of the noble gases on the periodic table
Each atom has seven valence electrons and gains one electron to form an ion with a −1 charge
Their name comes from Greek words meaning “salt-former”
React with metals such as sodium to make salts like sodium chloride, table salt
They exist as diatomic molecules such as F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, and I₂
At room temperature, fluorine and chlorine are gases, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid
Bromine is one of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature; the other is mercury
Iodine is a gray-black solid that turns into a violet vapor when heated; its name comes from the Greek for “violet”
Reactivity decreases going down the group; fluorine is the most reactive element of all
Their −1 ions are fluoride, chloride, bromide, and iodide
A more reactive one displaces a less reactive one from a salt: chlorine turns potassium bromide solution orange-brown
Chlorine disinfects pools and drinking water, fluoride fights tooth decay, and iodine is added to “iodized” salt
Fluorine is the most electronegative element
Their acids with hydrogen are strong, except hydrofluoric acid, which is weak but can etch glass
Two different members bond to each other in compounds like chlorine trifluoride and iodine heptafluoride
Chlorine has the highest electron affinity of any element, higher even than fluorine’s
The bond in a fluorine molecule is surprisingly weaker than the bond in a chlorine molecule
Henri Moissan isolated fluorine in 1886 by electrolysis and won the 1906 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
Carl Wilhelm Scheele first made chlorine in 1774; Humphry Davy proved it was an element and named it for its pale green color
Bernard Courtois found iodine in seaweed ash (1811); Antoine Balard announced bromine (1826), whose name comes from the Greek for “stench”
Astatine, first made at Berkeley in 1940, is radioactive and very rare; its name means “unstable”
Tennessine, element 117, was first made in 2010 by Russian and American scientists and named for Tennessee
Light-sensitive silver compounds of these elements made photographic film work; silver iodide is used to seed clouds
Thomas Midgley Jr. helped develop CFC refrigerants; the 1987 Montreal Protocol phased them out to protect the ozone layer
Some bright light bulbs use iodine or bromine to help their tungsten filaments last longer
Grignard reagents are made from magnesium and a carbon compound containing chlorine, bromine, or iodine
Roy Plunkett discovered Teflon, made of carbon and fluorine, in 1938

trap.title: The family, not one member
trap.body: Tossups on this group are packed with single-element clues, like fluorine’s reactivity, chlorine in pools, or bromine as a liquid, which tempts players to blurt one element’s name. But the question wants the whole family. The noble gases, one column to the right, are the other trap: they almost never react, while these elements are among the most reactive on the periodic table.
trap.fix: Listen for “these elements” or “this group,” and answer with the family name. Seven valence electrons, −1 ions, “salt-former,” and diatomic molecules mean this group; full outer shells, glowing neon signs, and almost no reactions mean the noble gases.
trap.line: Real answer line: Halogens (accept group 17 or group VIIA elements; prompt on group 7)

topics.name: Hydrogen
topics.kicker: Element 1 · The lightest and most common element in the universe
topics.briefing: Hydrogen is element number one: the lightest, simplest atom, usually just one proton and one electron. It makes up about three-quarters of the normal matter in the universe, and stars like the Sun shine by fusing it into helium. In 1937 the hydrogen-filled airship _Hindenburg_ burst into flames in New Jersey, but in a fuel cell, hydrogen makes a clean fuel whose only exhaust is water.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Radio astronomers map the spiral arms of the Milky Way using the 21-centimeter line, given off when the electron in an atom of this element flips its spin. This element’s visible spectral lines make up the Balmer series.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lightest element, which stars like the Sun fuse into helium.

tossups.p: Harold Urey won the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for discovering a heavier isotope of this element, deuterium, whose nucleus holds one proton and one neutron. Heavy water, used to slow down neutrons in some nuclear reactors, is made with that isotope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the most common in the universe, whose most common isotope has one proton and no neutrons.

tossups.p: James Dewar first turned this element into a liquid in 1898; in that form it boils at only about 20 kelvins. That liquid, burned with liquid oxygen, powered the main engines of NASA’s Space Shuttle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lightest element, which filled the German airship _Hindenburg_ when it burst into flames in 1937.

tossups.p: Molecules of this element come in two forms, ortho and para, depending on whether the spins of their two nuclei point the same way or opposite ways. Under crushing pressure, this element may become a liquid metal, as scientists think happens deep inside Jupiter.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this gas, the lightest element, which stars like the Sun fuse into helium.

tossups.p: This element’s atom is the only neutral atom for which the Schrödinger [“SHROH-ding-er”] equation can be solved exactly. In 1913, Niels Bohr explained the colors of light this element gives off with a model in which its single electron moves in fixed orbits.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 1, the most abundant element in the universe.

tossups.p: Henry Cavendish identified this element as a separate substance in 1766, calling it “inflammable air.” Antoine Lavoisier [“lah-vwah-zee-AY”] later named it using Greek words meaning “water-former,” because it makes water when it burns.
tossups.r: Two atoms of this element join one oxygen atom in each water molecule. For 10 points, name this element, the lightest of all.

tossups.p: Paul Sabatier [“sah-bah-TYAY”] won a Nobel Prize for discovering that finely powdered nickel helps this element add to carbon compounds, a reaction later used to turn liquid vegetable oils into solid margarine.
tossups.r: This element combines with nitrogen in the Haber process to make ammonia. For 10 points, name this lightest element.

tossups.p: When an electric current splits water, this element bubbles up at the negative electrode, with twice the volume of the oxygen produced at the other electrode. In the Haber process, nitrogen is combined with this element under high pressure to make ammonia.
tossups.r: This element gave the airship _Hindenburg_ its lift. For 10 points, name this lightest element, with atomic number 1.

tossups.p: Fuel cell cars combine this element with oxygen to make electricity, leaving only water as exhaust. In a school lab, a lit wooden splint makes a “squeaky pop” when it is held in a test tube full of this gas.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element with atomic number 1, the lightest of all.

tossups.p: This element is usually placed at the top of group 1, above lithium, even though it is a nonmetal and not an alkali metal. When an acid dissolves in water, it releases positive ions of this element, which are really just bare protons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, which makes up about three-quarters of the normal matter in the universe.

tossups.p: The Lyman series of spectral lines, which are all in the ultraviolet, comes from electrons in this element’s atoms falling to the lowest energy level. The Rydberg formula predicts the wavelengths of light given off by this element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, whose single electron Niels Bohr described in his 1913 model of the atom.

tossups.p: About 380,000 years after the Big Bang, the universe cooled enough for electrons and nuclei to combine into neutral atoms, most of them atoms of this element. Stars like the Sun shine by fusing this element’s nuclei into helium in their cores.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant element in the universe, which has atomic number 1.

tossups.p: The most common isotope of this element, sometimes called protium, is the only stable kind of atom whose nucleus contains no neutrons. Because its molecules are the lightest of all, this element’s gas escapes through tiny holes faster than any other gas.
tossups.r: The airship _Hindenburg_ was filled with this flammable gas when it burst into flames in 1937. For 10 points, name this element.

tossups.p: Tritium, a radioactive isotope of this element with two neutrons, has a half-life of about 12 years and is used to make some exit signs and watch dials glow. Tritium decays into a light form of helium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this element, the lightest of all, whose most common isotope has just one proton and no neutrons.

tossups.p: Emission nebulae such as the Orion Nebula glow pinkish red because of a bright line in this element’s Balmer series. The giant planets Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of this element, along with helium.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this most abundant element in the universe, which has atomic number 1.

clues.t: Element number 1: the lightest element, usually just one proton and one electron
Most abundant element in the universe, about three-quarters of normal matter by mass
Stars like the Sun fuse it into helium in their cores
Two of its atoms join one oxygen atom in every water molecule
The airship _Hindenburg_ was filled with it when it burst into flames in 1937
Henry Cavendish identified it as a separate substance in 1766, calling it “inflammable air”
Antoine Lavoisier named it from Greek words meaning “water-former”
Its three isotopes: protium (no neutrons), deuterium (one neutron), and radioactive tritium (two neutrons)
A colorless, odorless, highly flammable gas made of two-atom (diatomic) molecules
A lit splint makes a “squeaky pop” in a test tube of it
Fuel cells combine it with oxygen to make electricity, with only water as exhaust
Combined with nitrogen in the Haber process to make ammonia
Acids release its positive ions, which are just bare protons; pH measures how many there are
Electrolysis of water produces it at the negative electrode, twice the volume of the oxygen
Placed at the top of group 1 above lithium, though it is a nonmetal, not an alkali metal
Its visible spectral lines form the Balmer series; its ultraviolet Lyman series ends at the lowest energy level
Niels Bohr’s 1913 model explained its spectrum, which the Rydberg formula describes
Radio astronomers map the Milky Way with its 21-centimeter line, made when its electron flips its spin
Harold Urey discovered its isotope deuterium and won the 1934 Nobel Prize in Chemistry; heavy water is made with deuterium
James Dewar first liquefied it in 1898; the liquid boils at about 20 kelvins
Its liquid form, burned with liquid oxygen, powered the Space Shuttle’s main engines
Under crushing pressure it is predicted to become a liquid metal, thought to exist deep inside Jupiter and Saturn
Its molecules come in ortho and para forms, depending on whether their two nuclear spins are parallel or opposite
The only neutral atom for which the Schrödinger equation can be solved exactly
Paul Sabatier won a Nobel Prize for using powdered nickel to add it to carbon compounds, later used to turn vegetable oil into margarine
Radioactive tritium, with a half-life of about 12 years, makes some exit signs and watch dials glow
Emission nebulae such as the Orion Nebula glow pinkish red from one of its Balmer lines
Its gas escapes through tiny holes (effuses) faster than any other gas, because its molecules are the lightest

trap.title: Element, not isotope
trap.body: Many clues name this element’s isotopes, deuterium and tritium, or things named after it, like hydrogen bonds and the hydrogen bomb, and players blurt those instead. Helium is the other trap: it is the second element, the product of the Sun’s fusion, and the gas in modern party balloons and blimps.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this element,” name the element itself, even when the clue is about one of its isotopes. Atomic number 1, “water-former,” Cavendish, the Balmer series, and the _Hindenburg_ all point here; “second-lightest,” “noble gas,” or the product of the Sun’s fusion means helium.

topics.name: Water
topics.kicker: H₂O · The bent, polar molecule that covers most of Earth
topics.dates: Shown to be hydrogen plus oxygen in the 1780s
topics.briefing: Water is just two hydrogen atoms stuck to one oxygen atom, but it is one of the strangest substances around. Its bent, lopsided molecules cling to each other through hydrogen bonds, which lets water soak up huge amounts of heat and lets insects stand on its surface. Strangest of all, it expands when it freezes, so ice floats on top of lakes instead of sinking to the bottom.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Until 2019, the kelvin was defined using this substance’s triple point, the one temperature and pressure where its solid, liquid, and gas forms can all exist together. Anders Celsius’s original temperature scale put 100 degrees at this substance’s freezing point and 0 at its boiling point.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound whose molecules have two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

tossups.p: The ion product constant of this compound equals 1.0 times 10 to the negative 14th at 25 degrees Celsius, because a tiny fraction of its molecules split into hydronium and hydroxide ions. It is amphoteric, meaning it can act as either an acid or a base.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound, which has a pH of 7 when pure at room temperature.

tossups.p: The Mpemba [“em-PEM-bah”] effect is the claim that a hot sample of this substance can sometimes freeze faster than a cold one. On a phase diagram, the line between this substance’s solid and liquid forms slopes backward, so squeezing its solid form hard enough can make it melt.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this substance that freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

tossups.p: Each molecule of this compound can form up to four hydrogen bonds, which lock its solid form into an open, six-sided crystal pattern. Because of that open structure, this compound expands by about 9 percent when it freezes.
tossups.r: Its solid form, ice, floats on its liquid form. For 10 points, name this compound with a bent molecular shape.

tossups.p: In 1943, Norwegian commandos working with the Allies sabotaged a plant at Vemork, Norway, that made a “heavy” form of this compound in which deuterium replaces ordinary hydrogen. That heavy form can slow down neutrons inside nuclear reactors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound that covers about 71 percent of Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: Thales of Miletus [“mye-LEE-tus”] argued that everything in the world is ultimately made of this substance. Many centuries later, Henry Cavendish showed that it forms when hydrogen burns, and Antoine Lavoisier proved that it is a compound, not an element.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this substance that the ancient Greeks counted as one of the four classical elements, along with earth, air, and fire.

tossups.p: The kilogram was originally defined as the mass of one liter of this substance, and the calorie was defined as the energy needed to warm one gram of it by one degree Celsius.
tossups.r: This substance’s molecules are attracted to each other by hydrogen bonds. For 10 points, name this compound, often called the “universal solvent.”

tossups.p: This compound’s molecules have a bent shape with a bond angle of about 104.5 degrees, because its central oxygen atom has two lone pairs of electrons. That lopsided shape makes the molecule strongly polar.
tossups.r: This polar compound dissolves so many substances that it is called the “universal solvent.” For 10 points, name this compound, whose solid form, ice, floats.

tossups.p: Some insects, such as pond skaters, can stand on this liquid because of its high surface tension. Cohesion and adhesion let this liquid climb up narrow tubes in a process called capillary action.
tossups.r: Its molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds. For 10 points, name this liquid, which boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.

tossups.p: This compound has an unusually high specific heat: it takes about 4.18 joules to warm one gram of it by one degree Celsius, which helps oceans keep coastal climates mild. Its high heat of vaporization lets sweat cool the body as it evaporates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound, which freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and covers most of Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: During photosynthesis, plants split molecules of this compound in photosystem II, releasing their oxygen atoms as oxygen gas. Cellular respiration produces this compound when oxygen accepts electrons at the end of the electron transport chain.
tossups.r: Plants take in this compound through their roots. For 10 points, name this compound made of hydrogen and oxygen.

tossups.p: Passing an electric current through this compound in a process called electrolysis splits it into two gases, with twice as much hydrogen as oxygen by volume. An electrolyte such as dilute sulfuric acid is often added first, because the pure compound conducts electricity poorly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound, which makes up more than half of the human body by mass.

tossups.p: Condensation reactions, which link small molecules into larger ones such as proteins and starch, release one molecule of this compound each time a new bond forms. Breaking those bonds apart again requires adding this compound back.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound, which makes up most of a living cell.

tossups.p: This liquid is densest not at its freezing point but at about 4 degrees Celsius, so in winter the bottom of a deep lake stays near that temperature while its surface freezes.
tossups.r: Its polar molecules are attracted to each other through hydrogen bonds. For 10 points, name this compound, the most common liquid on Earth’s surface.

tossups.p: The Leidenfrost [“LYE-den-frost”] effect makes droplets of this liquid skitter across a very hot pan on a cushion of their own vapor. In Kurt Vonnegut’s novel _Cat’s Cradle_, ice-nine is a fictional solid form of this substance that stays frozen at room temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this compound that covers most of Earth’s surface and whose solid form is ice.

clues.t: Made of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom
Called the “universal solvent” because it dissolves so many substances
Its solid form, ice, is less dense than the liquid, so ice floats
Freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level
Covers about 71 percent of Earth’s surface
Bent molecule with a bond angle of about 104.5°, because the oxygen atom has two lone pairs
A polar molecule; its molecules stick together through hydrogen bonds
Very high specific heat: about 4.18 joules (1 calorie) warms 1 gram of it by 1 °C
High surface tension lets pond skaters stand on it; cohesion and adhesion cause capillary action
Densest at about 4 degrees Celsius, not at its freezing point
Electrolysis splits it into hydrogen and oxygen gas, 2 to 1 by volume
Pure samples are neutral, with a pH of 7 at 25 °C
Amphoteric: it can act as either an acid or a base
Plants split it in photosynthesis, releasing oxygen, and cellular respiration produces it
Released when condensation (dehydration synthesis) reactions build big molecules; added back to break them apart in hydrolysis
Its ion product constant, Kw, is 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, as a few molecules split into hydronium and hydroxide ions
Its triple point was used to define the kelvin until 2019
The kilogram was first defined as the mass of one liter of it, and the calorie as the heat to warm 1 gram of it by 1 °C
Anders Celsius’s original scale put 100 at its freezing point and 0 at its boiling point
In 1943, commandos sabotaged a plant at Vemork, Norway, that made its “heavy” form, which uses deuterium
The Mpemba effect claims a hot sample can sometimes freeze faster than a cold one
On its phase diagram, the solid–liquid line slopes backward, so pressure can melt its solid form
Each molecule can form four hydrogen bonds, giving ice an open, six-sided crystal; it expands about 9 percent when it freezes
Thales of Miletus said everything is made of it; it was one of the four classical elements
Henry Cavendish showed it forms when hydrogen burns; Antoine Lavoisier showed it is a compound, not an element
Leidenfrost effect: droplets skitter across a very hot pan on a cushion of their own vapor
Kurt Vonnegut’s _Cat’s Cradle_ features ice-nine, a fictional solid form that stays frozen at room temperature

trap.title: Water, ice, or hydrogen?
trap.body: Clues about floating ice, the triple point, or ice-nine tempt players to say “ice,” but “ice” names only the solid form, and the question usually wants the whole substance. Other players hear “hydrogen bonds” or “two hydrogen atoms” and blurt “hydrogen,” which is just one element in the molecule. “Heavy water” is a different compound, made with deuterium.
trap.fix: If the question says “this compound,” “this substance,” or “this liquid,” say water (or H₂O). Save “ice” for questions that ask for “this solid,” and “hydrogen bonds” for questions about the attraction itself.
trap.line: Real answer line: Water (accept H2O or dihydrogen monoxide; prompt on ice or steam)
